title: Ratios & percents
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Stuck? Open a hint. A wrong answer shows why, and every problem has a worked solution.

problems.prompt: What is $35\%$ of $240$?
A price rose from $\$80$ to $\$92$. By what percent did it rise?

mistakes.why: That is the rise in dollars. Divide it by the OLD price and multiply by $100$.

problems.prompt: Red and blue marbles are in the ratio $3 : 5$. There are $64$ marbles. How many are blue?

mistakes.why: That is the red marbles: $3$ of the $8$ parts.

problems.solution: One part is $\frac{64}{8} = 8$ marbles; blue is $5$ parts: $40$.

problems.prompt: After a $20\%$ discount, a game costs $\$36$. What was the original price, in dollars?

mistakes.why: $\$36$ is $80\%$ of the original: divide by $0.8$ instead of adding $20\%$.

hints: After $20\%$ off, $80\%$ of the price is left.

title: Ratios & percents: PSAT questions
instructions: Four PSAT-style questions with choices (A) to (D), easiest first. You can leave a question blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set, and you'll see a worked solution for each question.

problems.prompt: A recipe uses $2$ cups of flour for $12$ cookies. How many cups are needed for $30$ cookies?
A shirt costs $\$40$. Its price goes up $10\%$, then the new price goes down $10\%$. What is the final price, in dollars?

why.C: The $10\%$ decrease is taken from the higher price, $\$44$.
why.D: That is the price after the increase only.

problems.prompt: A runner covers $1500$ metres in $5$ minutes. What is the speed in kilometres per hour?

why.D: That is metres per minute. Change to km per hour.
why.A: $1.5$ km in $5$ minutes is $12$ lots of $5$ minutes in an hour.

problems.solution: $1500$ m $= 1.5$ km in $\frac{5}{60}$ hour: $1.5 \times 12 = 18$ km/h, choice (C).

problems.prompt: In a class, $40\%$ of the students walk to school. If $18$ students walk, how many students are in the class?

why.A: That is $40\%$ of $18$. Here $18$ is the $40\%$.

title: Statistics
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Stuck? Open a hint. A wrong answer shows why, and every problem has a worked solution.

problems.prompt: What is the mean of $7$, $11$, $4$, $15$ and $8$?
What is the median of $3$, $9$, $14$, $6$, $11$ and $20$?

mistakes.why: Put the values in order first.

hints: With six values, take the mean of the middle two.
problems.solution: In order: $3, 6, 9, 11, 14, 20$. The middle two are $9$ and $11$, so the median is $10$.

problems.prompt: The mean of six numbers is $15$. Five of them are $10$, $12$, $18$, $20$ and $14$. What is the sixth?

mistakes.why: Turn the mean into a total first: $6 \times 15 = 90$.

hints: The six numbers add up to $6 \times 15 = 90$.
The five you know add up to $74$.
problems.solution: Total $= 90$; the five add to $74$; the sixth is $90 - 74 = 16$.

problems.prompt: The data set $5, 8, 9, 12, 16$ gets a new value, $30$. By how much does the range increase?
problems.solution: Old range $16 - 5 = 11$; new range $30 - 5 = 25$. It increases by $14$.

title: Statistics: PSAT questions
instructions: Four PSAT-style questions with choices (A) to (D), easiest first. You can leave a question blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set, and you'll see a worked solution for each question.

problems.prompt: Which change to the data set $2, 4, 6, 8, 100$ would change its median?
problems.solution: The median is $6$. Adding $50$ makes six values, $2, 4, 6, 8, 50, 100$, with median $\frac{6 + 8}{2} = 7$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: The mean of $5$ numbers is $20$. When one number is removed, the mean of the other four is $18$. What number was removed?

why.A: Compare the totals, not the means: $100 - 72$.

problems.solution: Totals: $5 \times 20 = 100$ and $4 \times 18 = 72$. The removed number is $28$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: Data set A is $10, 20, 30, 40, 50$ and data set B is $28, 29, 30, 31, 32$. Which statement is true?

choices: They have the same mean, and A has the larger standard deviation.
They have the same mean, and B has the larger standard deviation.

why.B: B’s values are bunched near $30$, so its spread is smaller.

problems.solution: Both have mean $30$. A’s values are much farther from $30$, so A has the larger standard deviation, choice (A).

problems.prompt: Researchers chose $200$ adults at random in one city and found that those who walk every day tend to have lower blood pressure. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices: Walking every day lowers blood pressure for all adults.
Walking every day lowers blood pressure for adults in that city.
In that city, adults who walk every day tend to have lower blood pressure.
In every city, adults who walk every day have lower blood pressure.

why.A: This was not an experiment, so it can’t show cause, and the sample is from one city only.
why.B: This was not an experiment: it shows a link, not that walking causes it.
why.D: The sample came from one city only.

problems.solution: A random sample lets you generalise to that city, but an observational study shows a link, not cause and effect: choice (C).

title: Probability
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Stuck? Open a hint. A wrong answer shows why, and every problem has a worked solution.

problems.prompt: A bag has $4$ red, $6$ blue and $10$ green counters. One is picked at random. What is the probability it is blue?
The probability of rain tomorrow is $0.35$. What is the probability it does not rain?
Of $120$ people surveyed, $45$ prefer tea, and $27$ of the tea drinkers are under $30$. A tea drinker is picked at random. What is the probability they are under $30$?

mistakes.why: "A tea drinker is picked": divide by the $45$ tea drinkers, not everyone.

hints: Only the $45$ tea drinkers can be picked.

problems.prompt: A fair coin is flipped and a fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability of heads and a number greater than $4$?

mistakes.why: For two independent events, MULTIPLY the probabilities.

title: Probability: PSAT questions
instructions: Four PSAT-style questions with choices (A) to (D), easiest first. You can leave a question blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set, and you'll see a worked solution for each question.

problems.prompt: A spinner has $8$ equal sections numbered $1$ to $8$. What is the probability of spinning a number greater than $5$?

why.D: That is the probability of $5$ or less.
why.C: Greater than $5$ means $6$, $7$ or $8$: three sections.

problems.prompt: In a school, $60$ students take Spanish and $40$ take French; no one takes both. $15$ of the Spanish students and $10$ of the French students are in Grade 10. A Grade 10 student is picked at random. What is the probability they take French?

why.B: That is the fraction of French students in Grade 10. Here you pick from the Grade 10 students.
why.D: Compare the French students with ALL $25$ Grade 10 students, not with the Spanish ones.

problems.solution: There are $15 + 10 = 25$ Grade 10 students and $10$ take French: $\frac{10}{25} = \frac{2}{5}$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: A quality check finds that $2\%$ of light bulbs are faulty. About how many faulty bulbs would you expect in a batch of $1500$?
Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that both show a $6$?

why.D: For independent events, multiply the probabilities: don’t add them.
why.C: That is the chance for one die.
